1.pericope_label: For we know that, if our earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens

schools.summary: Read the imagery from Paul's own trade as a tentmaker and from the grammar — the genitive is appositive, the house simply is the tent, the verb is the one used for striking a tent, and the possession is present, held now by title. On the promised building, weigh the spiritual body against a celestial vehicle for the intermediate state and object that Scripture says nothing of such a vehicle.

Take the body as both a curious piece of architecture arguing its architect and the soul's lodging, which shows the soul independent of it; and ground the opening verb in revelation rather than intellect, since the heathen had notions of immortality but no assurance — Cicero's reader assents while he reads and loses it when he lays the book down.

Read the dissolution through the Mosaic tabernacle, taken to pieces in transit with the ark carried separately under its own covering, and infer that the soul must have some vehicle to subsist in until it receives its body again.

Turn the decay of the outward man into an argument for gladness: since its destruction conducts us to immortality, one ought not merely to avoid grieving at its partial ruin but to seek its completion.

Distinguish the two things the opening verb covers — assurance of a future blessedness, and a good hope through grace of one's own interest in it — and set the whole under the precept given to the sons of Noah.

debates.question: What is the building of God not made with hands?

sides.position: The future spiritual body
A vehicle in which the soul subsists between death and the resurrection
The blessed state of the soul after death, of which the risen body is the consummation
Scripture says nothing of any such intermediate vehicle

outliers.note: Alone argues the point from pagan literature, citing Cicero’s reader who assents while reading and loses the conviction on closing the book, and Seneca’s judgement that immortality was promised rather than proved.
Alone reconstructs the dissolution from the dismantling of the Mosaic tabernacle, and alone infers from it a vehicle for the disembodied soul.

2.pericope_label: For in this we groan, earnestly desiring to be clothed upon with our house which is from heaven: if so be that being clothed we shall not be found naked

schools.summary: Mark the change of figure from dwelling to garment as a real mixed metaphor, note the classical parallels for both, and read the difficult clause about not being found naked as meaning that the soul will not be bodiless — with the Greek particles asserting rather than conceding, since to a Greek the world of the dead was a place of shadows and Paul is certain nothing there is unreal.

Refer the supposition to the saints alive at Christ's coming, who are never stripped at all; and dissent from those who find nothing new in the clause, reading instead a twofold clothing — the righteousness of Christ and sanctification now, immortality and glory afterwards.

Insist that the expressions are Jewish and must be read as the Jews used them, marshalling the rabbinic usage in which clothing means investiture of any kind and "house" denotes a case or covering, so that being clothed with a house may name a settled quality of the soul.

debates.question: What does "if so be that being clothed we shall not be found naked" mean?

sides.position: That the soul will not be bodiless, but clothed in its glorified body
That the saints alive at Christ's coming are never stripped of the body at all
That a twofold clothing is meant, Christ's righteousness now and immortality afterwards
That the man will not be found destitute of the divine image

debates.question: How far should the rabbinic material about garments of the soul be used?

sides.position: It is the key to the passage, since the expressions are Jewish
They are trifles, and Paul refers to nothing of the kind

outliers.note: Alone treats the rabbinic doctrine of garments of the soul as the interpretative key, where Barnes, working from the same collection, dismisses it as trifles.

4.pericope_label: For we that are in this tabernacle do groan, being burdened: not for that we would be unclothed, but clothed upon, that mortality might be swallowed up of life. Now he that hath wrought us for the selfsame thing is God, who also hath given unto us the earnest of the Spirit

schools.summary: Correct the placing of the negative — Paul does not wish to put the clothing off at all, but to put more on, having no desire to be a disembodied spirit — and read the whole as the expectation of a man who thought the Coming near and hoped to be changed rather than to die.

Concede the natural aversion to quitting life, as no one is willingly stripped of his clothes, and let confidence overcome it in the way a man parts readily from a tattered garment for a new one; and trace the longing itself to God, since natural feeling never reaches it.

Refuse to make affliction the motive: we would not die an hour before the time God has assigned, whatever tribulation we pass through, and faith does not share the philosophical contempt for what the Creator has given. Find in the longing after immortality the evidence of the divinity that stirs within us.
Cite the verse about the earnest of the Spirit among proofs that Paul and the apostles were full of the Holy Spirit.

sides.position: Under the burden of a particular bodily affliction, not merely the weariness of life
Because believers know themselves exiles, shut up in the body as in a prison
Under the numberless afflictions, infirmities and temptations of the present state

outliers.note: Alone quotes English verse — Addison’s lines on the longing after immortality — as a paraphrase of the apostle’s sense.
Alone reads the groaning as evidence of a particular illness, and alone notes the close parallel in the Wisdom of Solomon.

6.pericope_label: Therefore we are always confident, knowing that, whilst we are at home in the body, we are absent from the Lord: for we walk by faith, not by sight

schools.summary: Recover the force of two rare verbs, contrasted in the papyri as being among one's own people and being abroad, and correct the famous clause: the word rendered "sight" never means the faculty of seeing but the form of the thing seen, so the sense is not by appearance.

Resolve the apparent contradiction that God is everywhere said to be with us while Paul says we are absent from him, by distinguishing his upholding presence and his indwelling by the Spirit from the face-to-face vision we still lack; and set the believer's contentment against the unbeliever's perpetual ferment.

Make heaven the Christian's country while the body remains the soul's present lodging, and read the verse as leaving no interval between being in the body and being with the Lord in which the soul might sleep.

sides.position: Yes — the word never means the faculty of seeing, but the appearance of the thing seen
The traditional wording will serve; the point is that the Christian orders his life by things unseen

outliers.note: Alone turns the verse into a polemic against those who deny the soul’s separate existence, remarking that Paul learned no such philosophy from Gamaliel or in the third heaven.

8.pericope_label: We are confident, I say, and willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord. Wherefore we labour, that, whether present or absent, we may be accepted of him

schools.summary: Reconcile the preference stated here with the earlier refusal to be unclothed by weakening the expression — content to accept death if it comes first — and suggest as an alternative that Paul means the ecstatic state in which he could not tell whether he was in the body or out of it; then render the next verb as ambition rather than labour.

Take the clause as proof that souls released from the body live in God's presence, and infer that true faith produces not merely contempt of death but desire for it, so that dread outweighing hope is a token of unbelief — with the limit that believers do not try to anticipate their Lord's day.
Read the preference as a Christian's proper choice of glory over suffering while refusing to wish for death before its time, and make the pleasing of God itself the substance of heaven.
State the corollary that well-grounded hopes of heaven do not encourage sloth or sinful security.

debates.question: How can Paul prefer to be out of the body here, having refused to be unclothed earlier?

sides.position: The expression here is weaker: content to accept death if it comes before the Coming
Possibly he means the ecstatic state in which he could not tell whether he was in the body
Faith produces not merely contempt of death but desire for it, without anticipating the Lord's day

outliers.note: Alone suggests that the preference may refer to Paul’s ecstatic experiences rather than to death, resting the case on the tense of the two verbs.

10.pericope_label: For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, that every one may receive the things done in his body. Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men; but we are made manifest unto God

schools.summary: Restore "be made manifest" for "appear," supply the Roman tribunal behind the word for judgment seat, and read the clause about receiving according to one's deeds as an unqualified assertion of retribution that no theological formula may be allowed to soften.

Describe the day in its particulars — the summons, the thrones, the opened books, the sentence — and answer the charge of inconsistency by distinguishing the two recompenses: evil deeds are requited as deserved, while good deeds are rewarded only because God, having first accepted the person of unmerited goodness, then graciously accepts his works.

Object that "terror" is too harsh for a phrase that means the fear of the Lord, and turn the correction against preachers who justify constant declamation on hell by this text, sending them to learn from Christ's weeping over Jerusalem.
Draw from the same knowledge a stricter rule of ministry — not merely giving no handle of offence, but declining to repel a false suspicion even when it could be repelled.

debates.question: Is "the terror of the Lord" a sound rendering?

sides.position: No — it means the fear of the Lord, reverence rather than dread, and "terror" first entered in the Geneva version
The older word may stand, provided it is noticed that Paul persuades rather than frightens

debates.question: Can a judgment according to works be reconciled with free forgiveness?

sides.position: The assertion of retribution is unqualified, and no theological formula may be allowed to soften it
Evil deeds are requited as deserved; good works are rewarded only because God first accepts the person of unmerited goodness

outliers.note: Alone attacks the “system-builders of theology” by name for evading the plain assertion of retribution, and alone supplies the Roman legal setting of the judgment seat.
Alone rebukes preachers who use this text to justify constant declamation on hell, and alone objects to “terror” as a rendering on lexical grounds.

12.pericope_label: For we commend not ourselves again unto you, but give you occasion to glory on our behalf, that ye may have somewhat to answer them which glory in appearance, and not in heart. For whether we be beside ourselves, it is to God

schools.summary: Hear the sentence as a flinch under a repeated sneer and read it as furnishing the Corinthians with materials for a reply rather than as self-praise; identify the rivals' boast as external, and suggest that men were contrasting their imposing presence with Paul's bodily weakness and small stature.

Make reputation a servant's concern only so far as it serves the church, and detect a reproach in the necessity — the Corinthians should have magnified his apostleship unasked. Treat the charge of madness as a concession spoken in the objectors' language, since he is content to be reckoned mad or sober so long as God is served.
Identify the opponent as a false apostle dividing the church, and hold that congregations generally prefer the calmer manner in their teachers, though teachers must obey God whoever is offended.
State the best defence a slandered ministry can have: that the word has been manifested to the hearers' consciences and made effectual to their conversion.

debates.question: What were the rivals glorying in?

sides.position: Rank, eloquence, talents and external advantages
Their orthodox Judaism
An imposing personal presence, set against Paul's bodily weakness and small stature
The standing of a particular false apostle who was dividing the church

outliers.note: Alone glosses the word Paul gives them as a base of operations — “as we say a tip, only much more.”

14.pericope_label: For the love of Christ constraineth us; because we thus judge, that if one died for all, then were all dead: and that he died for all, that they which live should not henceforth live unto themselves

schools.summary: Settle the genitive as Christ's love for us on the ground of Paul's usage elsewhere, and rule out the common reading of "then were all dead" on grammatical grounds, since the verb names a momentary act of dying rather than a state — so that the all died when the one died, the preposition bearing its ordinary substitutionary sense.

Read the constraint as a bond: no one who truly ponders that love can withhold himself, and Christ redeemed us to hold us as his own possession, so that we are no longer our own masters and may find it no hardship to be made nothing.

Take the universality of the death as beyond doubt and infer the universal death of men from it, since had any man been otherwise Christ need not have died for him; and picture the constraint as winds and tides bearing a vessel to its harbour.

sides.position: Christ's love toward us
Both his love to us and ours to him
Our love to him, awakened by his

debates.question: What does "then were all dead" assert?

sides.position: That all were already guilty and under sentence, which is why he had to die
That the all died when the one died; the verb is a momentary act of dying, not a state of death

outliers.note: Alone declines to choose between the two senses of the genitive, and supplies the image of winds and tides bearing a vessel to harbour.

16.pericope_label: Wherefore henceforth know we no man after the flesh: yea, though we have known Christ after the flesh, yet now henceforth know we him no more. Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new

schools.summary: Itemise the discarded standards — birth, country, rank, wealth, kindred — and explain the parenthesis about having known Christ after the flesh as pointing either to a Corinthian party claiming personal acquaintance with him or to Paul's own earlier expectation of an earthly Messiah; then insist that the last clause states a fact and not a duty.

Include under "flesh" every external endowment, and read the imperative instead — let him be a new creature — condemning learning and eloquence alike where renovation of heart is wanting. Guard the verse against Servetus, who used it to make Christ's humanity absorbed into his divinity.

Press the practical consequence in the sharpest form — we fear not the great, regard not the rich, account not the least less than ourselves — and describe the change as a new creation rather than a mending, only the power that makes a world being able to make a Christian.

Take the verse as teaching weanedness from the world, and infer that the bodily presence of Christ is not to be doted upon, so that images used in worship are not the appointed way of strengthening faith.

debates.question: Does the last clause state a fact or issue a command?

sides.position: A fact: the man in Christ is a new creation and will live like one
A command: let him who would hold a place in Christ's kingdom be a new creature
Both readings are current

debates.question: In what sense had Paul known Christ after the flesh?

sides.position: He had expected the Messiah as others did, with hopes of an earthly kingdom
He had judged Christ by the standards of the Sanhedrin before his conversion
Whether he had seen Christ at all is uncertain, and does not matter

outliers.note: Alone turns the verse against Servetus, who used it to argue that Christ’s humanity is now absorbed into his divinity.
Alone draws from the verse an argument against the use of images of Christ in worship.

18.pericope_label: And all things are of God, who hath reconciled us to himself by Jesus Christ, and hath given to us the ministry of reconciliation; to wit, that God was in Christ, reconciling the world unto himself, not imputing their trespasses unto them

schools.summary: Restrict "all things" by the article to the new creation just named, note this as the earliest use of the reconciling word for God's work in Christ, and decline to be troubled that a God who does not reckon trespasses is also said to judge according to works.

Identify the Father as the one who was in Christ, since it would be improper to say Christ's divine nature was in Christ, and read the incarnation as God drawing near after withdrawing — while holding that men return into favour precisely by being reckoned righteous through remission of sins.

Locate the whole obstacle in man: there is an enmity in the human heart against sacred things, and that enmity, not any reluctance in God, is the grand hindrance to salvation, the word for reconciling meaning to change thoroughly.

debates.question: How should "God was in Christ reconciling" be construed?

sides.position: God was in Christ — of the Father, not of Christ's divine nature; his coming is God's drawing near
God was reconciling in Christ a world unto himself, both nouns being anarthrous
God acted by means of Christ, or was united to Christ and manifested in him

outliers.note: Alone dates the vocabulary, observing that this is the earliest place in Paul’s letters where the reconciling word describes God’s work in Christ, and counts its occurrences across the epistles of the period.

20.pericope_label: Now then we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God did beseech you by us: we pray you in Christ's stead, be ye reconciled to God

schools.summary: Trace the title from the Greek word for an elder to the Emperor's legate in the inscriptions, and note that "ambassador" first enters English here in the version of 1611; then mark what Paul does not say — no wrath of the Father averted by the Son, no penalty exacted as a quantitative equivalent, the whole originating in the Father's love.

Deny that the envoys propose terms at all, holding that they proclaim a peace already made; and ground the embassy's authority in divine ordination, since no one would rest his salvation on a man's promise — from which follows a hard judgement on ministers who never discharge it.

Set the chain of representation out plainly, Christ representing the Father and the apostles Christ, and fasten on the wonder of the beseeching: no judge ever begged a condemned criminal to accept a pardon, nor a creditor a ruined debtor to receive an acquittance.

debates.question: What are the ambassadors authorised to do?

sides.position: To explain and enforce the terms on which God is willing to be reconciled
Not to propose terms or treat at all, but to proclaim a peace already made

outliers.note: Quotes Wesley’s note on this verse verbatim and by name, and then Charles Wesley’s hymn on it, so that the apparent agreement of the two wesleyan-arminian witnesses here is quotation rather than independent judgement.
Alone turns the verse into a judgement on the hierarchy of his own day, calling ministers who never discharge the embassy dumb idols.

21.pericope_label: For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him

schools.summary: Assert the sinlessness as absolute — Christ alone learned sin's power by resisting it — and reject the sin-offering rendering as foreign to the New Testament, holding that God dealt with him as though he were sin itself; then read "the righteousness of God" as the divine attribute shared by identification with Christ, the purpose of the death being not chiefly escape from punishment but the becoming righteous.

State the imputation in its strongest form, that Christ was treated as not merely a sinner but a mass of sin, and make the two halves of the verse measure each other: we are righteous in God's sight in the same respect in which Christ was a sinner, his condemnation being our absolution.

Render the word as sin-offering on Septuagint usage and charge the English version with founding on a mistranslation the doctrine that Christ became a proper object of divine indignation; take the righteousness as first imputed and then implanted.

debates.question: Does "made him to be sin" mean made him a sin-offering?

sides.position: Yes, on Septuagint usage; the contrary reading founds a blasphemous doctrine on a mistranslation
Yes in substance, though Christ was neither sin in the abstract, nor a sinner, nor guilty
No — that sense is foreign to the New Testament; God dealt with him as though he were sin itself
He was made sin by imputation, and treated as a mass of sin

outliers.note: Alone lists the Septuagint passages at length to prove the sin-offering sense, and alone accuses the English version of founding a blasphemous doctrine on its rendering.
Alone connects the verse with the cry of dereliction from the cross, while warning against probing the mystery too far.
